Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
We look at how skipper John Matambu vanished at sea and why his alleged murder continues to evade justice.

Unique Selling Point:
With exclusive interviews, tons of B-roll, and other exclusive footage, viewers will feel as if they are tracking Ferdi Visser and piecing together John's disappearance themselves.

Summary:
A respected fisherman. A fugitive on the run. A boat that vanished—only to resurface, torched and abandoned on a remote Mozambican beach.
This is not just a story about a man who disappeared at sea. It’s a story about a system that failed—again and again.
In this investigation, Carte Blanche exposes the glaring gaps in the justice system that allowed convicted fraudster Ferdi Visser to manipulate the law, evade parole, and escape custody—not once, but twice.
How did a known fugitive manage to slip through the cracks so easily? And with Visser still on the run, will authorities finally be held accountable?

Press Release:


A popular and well-respected fisherman disappears at sea. His boat is found, torched and abandoned, on a remote Mozambican beach. A suspect slips through authorities’ fingers and goes on the run. It’s a story about a senseless murder, a known fugitive, and a broken system that has allowed a convicted fraudster to manipulate the law and skip parole – not once, but twice. Carte Blanche pieces together the mystery, traces the steps of an alleged murderer and asks: who will be held accountable?

So I say to him, listen, the wind's going to start picking up at about one. So he said, “Okay, so shortly I must start turning around to head back to Sodwana.” And ja, that was the last time I spoke to him.

UPS - JANINE INTERVIEW
I thought maybe engine problems or the steering packed up.

CHERIE: And I just remember gasping for breath and thinking, oh my God, what do you mean, “it's bad”? Tell me, he said, “John's missing”. What do you mean he’s missing? They said, “He hasn't come home.”

UPS: NEWS INSERT: Our hopes are that both men are found safe, and that this has all been a misunderstanding.

DECEPTION LINK
It was in the early stages of the search that the mysterious “Andre Cilliers” was revealed as Ferdi Visser — a convicted fraudster who’d absconded after being released on parole just 10 days before the fishing trip.

VO: Visser was supposed to serve two years in prison for an unrelated case of fraud. The search soon turned into a cross-border criminal investigation.

UPS: RICHARD INTERVEIW:
RICHARD: Die volgende ooggend toe bel 'n vriend my, toe sê hy kyk op die groep, op social media, daar's jou boot. // SUBTITLES: The next morning,a friend called me and said, “Look at the group, on social media. There's your boat”.

UPS: MARCUS JOUBERT INTERVIEW: The way that I found the boat, it just sent shivers down my spine, and I knew that that boat was burnt on the beach, it wasn't burnt at sea.

VO: Marcus was convinced this wasn’t the work of an experienced skipper.

UPS: MARCUS: The motors were still in gear. If John had burned that boat, the motors would have been in neutral...So these are all small little things that I concluded to say that a skipper didn't beach this boat.

LOURENSA: Initially when you still had hope and you didn't quite know what had happened to John, what role did social media and the community play in trying to find John?

VO: Visser’s image was widely shared online.

UPS: MARCUS: Right, now we’ve got a picture, we’ve got a name and it’s on social media

VO: Then, four days after the boat was discovered, a breakthrough:

UPS: MARCUS: Once we apprehended Visser…. It was, it was unbelievable how that happened. It was like watching a movie.

VO: Visser had been tracked down in Mozambique’s capital, Maputo. Not by the police, but… the community. Richard went to Maputo to identify Visser.

UPS: LOURENSA: Hoe was hy in daai oomblik gewees?

LOURENSA: Emosieloos?
Richard; Heeltemal.Toe vra hulle vir my of ek vir hom 'n vraag wil vra. Toe sê ek ja, ek wil net by hom weet waar's John? Toe sê hy vir my, nee, hy het John R20 000 gegee en John het hom in Ponta afgelaai en daarna weet hy nie verder nie.

VISSER THE CRIMINAL REFLECTIVE LINK: So, I’m just going through a list of all the charges that’s been brought against Ferdi Visser over the years, it’s quite extensive and it crosses borders. It includes theft, common assault, fraud, more common assault…

VO: Many of these cases are still open.

UPS: PAUL MOSTERT INTERVIEW: He obviously knows that he's got the might of the law ahead of him.

UPS: PAUL MOSTERT:
He was a very clever guy. He knew how to manipulate people.
He knew how to win your confidence over. And he knows how to get himself out of a lot of stuff.
I received numerous of calls from a lot of guys throughout South Africa that were taken with fraud by Ferdi Visser and I roughly added it up.
It came very close to about 8 or 9 million rand.
VO: Many questions remain about Visser’s motives. Could he be running from more than just the law?

COURT LINK: Following his arrest in Mozambique, Visser was extradited and was scheduled to appear in court in KZN in late May last year. John’s family, friends and other supporters travelled from near and far, determined to see Visser in court.
UPS CROWD: Legend of Sodwana!
VO: Our producers were there too.
UPS VOX POPS:
Producer: So why are you two here today?
Janine: To see Visser and to see if we can get some answers from him.
Frank: I want to know what they do to John Matambu
VO: John’s supporters waited… but Visser never arrived.
VO: The hearing proceeded despite Visser’s absence. He was facing charges of fraud and the theft of the boat.
UPS: MAGISTRATE: The accused in the matter is Thomas Frederick Visser,

VO: John’s supporters were dealt another unexpected blow.

UPS: MAGISTRATE: The charges against the accused are withdrawn in absentia.

UPS: People in the crowd shouting: What? Are you serious? No way!
All chant: Justice for John!

VO: Visser had allegedly injured himself on the way to court.

UPS: CHERIE: And today, the coward didn't face us. He hit his head so that they would take him to our hospital because he couldn't face us, so that's what we're dealing with.

UPS: JANINE: Bring him back here, now, today.
JANINE: Patch him up and bring him back.
JANINE: We’re here!

VO: The fraud and theft charges were withdrawn after the authorities bungled the extradition, moving Visser from Mozambique back into South Africa.

VO: Though the NPA confirmed the investigation is still ongoing it was devastating news for John’s friends and family.

UPS CHERIE: We know the only person who knows what has happened to John is this man Visser and we handed him to the authorities on a platter…

UPS CHERIE INTERVIEW: We just needed the system to do its job. And the system let us down in every way.
Lourensa: Is that why you decided to contact Advocate Gerrie Nel? Cherie: Yes, 100%.

VO: Gerrie Nel, who famously prosecuted disgraced Paralympian, Oscar Pistorius, now represents John Matambu’s family.

UPS: GERRIE INTERVIEW
Gerrie: We then met with Cherie and she, she compiled an impressive docket.
Lourensa: What went wrong with the extradition? Do we know?
Gerrie: We don't know, and I wish we did.
If something goes wrong, we start playing the blame game. The NPA would say, we blame the police. The police would say, we blame the NPA. Where as they should all work together to ensure that justice is done.

VO: The NPA confirmed that proper extradition procedures weren’t followed. They were not made aware of Visser’s arrest in Mozambique.

VO: Because Visser had absconded from his parole, he was sent back to prison to serve the remainder of his original fraud sentence.
VO: For months, Cherie and Adv. Nel pushed for something more. Not just justice… but accountability.
VO: They believed there was enough evidence to open a murder case.

UPS: GERRIE INTERVIEW
It's really easy. Two people got on a boat. One got off. Where's the other one?

VO: And then — just as it seemed they might be getting somewhere with John’s case —

UPS: CHERIE INTERVIEW
I then received a phone call from the investigation officer to say I have bad news…

I’m sorry…(CRYING)

ESCAPE LINK: Visser had escaped. Again. By the time authorities acknowledged it, he already had a 6-week head start.

UPS JANINE INTERVIEW
LOURENSA: Have you lost faith in the authorities?
JANINE: Oh, ja. Yeah. No faith in them, ja..
LOURENSA: How does that make you feel?
JANINE: Disgusted, absolutely disgusted that he's actually out of jail. That he was paroled. It should never have happened. But that's the justice system.

VO: In February this year, nearly a year after John disappeared, authorities finally acted.
VO: The South African Police Service confirmed they’ve closed the missing persons case, opened a murder investigation, and obtained a warrant for Visser’s arrest.
UPS: Singing in background: John, John, John, John Matambu, the legend of Sodwana Bay..

VO: A murder case may finally be open — but for John Matambu’s loved ones, it’s far from closure. The suspect remains at large, and the system continues to fail those left behind.

UPS: CHERIE IN GARDEN:
LOURENSA: So this is what you brought back from Mozambique? This is the wreck?
Cherie: It's just so tragic that it's gone from being his office to being your word, a wreck. It's more than that. This is John's coffin.

LOURENSA: And if you could say anything to Ferdi Visser?
CHERIE: I would tell him that he's not going to get away with murder. I now understand where the expression comes from. It comes from the broken justice system. It comes from people like Ferdi Visser who are repeat criminals, who know that they can fly under the radar because the justice system isn't together enough to bring them in and apprehend them. And I would tell him that he picked the wrong fisherman, that he picked the legend of Sodwana and he made a big mistake.

UPS:
John Matambu: Let’s go boys!
Thank you.

Carte Blanche HD nombuso@carteblanche.co.za 12 May 2025 TX Date: 0000-00-00 Press Release: A popular and well-respected fisherman disappears at sea. His boat is found, torched and abandoned, on a remote Mozambican beach. A suspect slips through authorities’ fingers and goes on the run. It’s a story about a senseless murder, a known fugitive, and a broken system that has allowed a convicted fraudster to manipulate the law and skip parole – not once, but twice. Carte Blanche pieces together the mystery, traces the steps of an alleged murderer and asks: who will be held accountable? Producers: Beth Neale & Miles Cloutier | Presenter: Lourensa Eckard Script: THE LAST CAST SCRIPT VO: Sodwana Bay in northern KwaZulu-Natal: a tight-knit community shaped by the sea… VO: One of the country’s premiere fishing destinations. UPS: John Matambu: Final day of OET. We need these fish. We really need them. RADIO: Somebody call it in. VO: Thirty years ago, John Matambu Dercksen left behind the bustle of Johannesburg for the open sea, later becoming a revered fisherman and sea captain. He made a living doing what he loved — taking people fishing. UPS: (Celebration) VO: But a year ago, a routine trip took a mysterious turn when neither John nor his client returned. UPS: NEWS INSERT: We got… alerted that charter vessel, ski boat, Magnum Too went missing at sea in uncertain circumstances SABC …it remains unknown what has happened, it’s a mystery… VO: What at first appeared a tragic accident …later became far more bewildering: the man John took fishing that day was not who he claimed to be. ESTABLISHING LINK: This is a story about family, community and belonging. It’s about an affable fisherman and the system that continues to fail his legacy. UPS: Court outrage: Justice for John! Justice for John! VO: For the past year, we’ve followed this unresolved case. VO: We’ve spoken to those who knew John Matambu, filming key moments, and piecing together the story. VO: John was given the name Matambu — inspired by the Zulu word for bones, reflecting his tall, slim build. UPS: Behind the scenes: 5, 4, 3, 2 and go for it. VO: For the past year, we’ve followed this unresolved case. VO: We’ve spoken to those who knew John Matambu, filming key moments, and piecing together the story. VO: John was given the name Matambu — inspired by the Zulu word for bones, reflecting his tall, slim build. UPS: “Here we’ve got worms, worms!” VO: He was deeply respected and loved in his community. UPS: John Laughs RADIO: Good afternoon, Matambu. You have permission to beach. UPS AYANDA NOMONDLA: No one got a problem with Matambu. No one fights with Matambu. Matambu is just a man, good, good man. VO: John freelanced as a skipper for a chartering company owned by Richard Scott. It was one of his boats that was hired on the 16th of March last year. UPS RICHARD SCOTT INTERVIEW LOURENSA: Richard so hierdie is amper soos die boot waarmee John-hulle uit is daai dag? // SUBTITLES: Richard, so this is similar to the boat that John and them went out on that day? RICHARD: Ja, presies dieselfde. Presies so gelyk. Net ‘n ander kleur. Die ou het my geskakel en die naam Andre, André Ciliers, of so iets Hy het hierdie brain tumor en sy vrou en sy dogter wil net vir oulaas see toe gaan. // SUBTITLES: Exactly the same. Looked exactly like this, just a different colour. The guy called me, with the name Andre, Andre Cilliers, or something like that. He apparently had this brain tumour and his wife and daughter just want to go out to sea for the last time. Lourensa: Daai dag wat jy hom gesien het op die strand, wat hy sy verskyning gemaak het, vertel my weer daarvan? // SUBTITLES: That day you saw him on the beach, when he made his appearance, tell me about it again. Richard: Dit het my baie gepla. Dis die eerste keer dat ek terug gegaan het vir my mense gesê het hierdie storie vandag pla my. // SUBTITLES: As I said, it bothered me a lot. It was the first time I went back and told my people that this story from today troubles me. Lourensa: Wat was die storie wat hy vertel het? // SUBTITLES: What was the story he told? Richard: Nee, dat sy vrou later gaan kom en sy gaan betaal // SUBTITLES: No, that his wife was coming later and she was going to pay VO: Richard was on the beach as John and his client set off into the surf… VO: A few hours into the trip, John called his fiancée, Janine Shaw. UPS: JANINE INTERVIEW - He phoned me to find out when the wind was going to start picking up, because he was up north at Island Rock. So. And it's about an hour's, drive to get back to Sodwana VO: Janine was waiting at John’s favourite bar where he’d meet her after every charter for a beer. UPS: JANINE INTERVIEW - MAAK ‘N JOL So I say to him, listen, the wind's going to start picking up at about one. So he said, “Okay, so shortly I must start turning around to head back to Sodwana.” And ja, that was the last time I spoke to him. VO: But as the hours passed and John didn’t return, it was clear something was wrong. UPS - JANINE INTERVIEW I thought maybe engine problems or the steering packed up. So initially I thought that was the problem and that we'd find him. VO: John’s sister, Cherie, was in Australia when she got a worrying call. UPS CHERIE: And I just remember gasping for breath and thinking, oh my God, what do you mean, “it's bad”? Tell me, he said, “John's missing”. What do you mean he’s missing? They said, “He hasn't come home.” VO: The community joined the police, Interpol, Crime Intelligence, NSRI and Border Patrol in the search for John Matambu, and his client, Andre Cilliers. UPS: NEWS INSERT: Our hopes are that both men are found safe, and that this has all been a misunderstanding. DECEPTION LINK It was in the early stages of the search that the mysterious “Andre Cilliers” was revealed as Ferdi Visser — a convicted fraudster who’d absconded after being released on parole just 10 days before the fishing trip. VO: Visser was supposed to serve two years in prison for an unrelated case of fraud. The search soon turned into a cross-border criminal investigation. UPS: RICHARD INTERVEIW: RICHARD: Die volgende ooggend toe bel 'n vriend my, toe sê hy kyk op die groep, op social media, daar's jou boot. // SUBTITLES: The next morning,a friend called me and said, “Look at the group, on social media. There's your boat”. LOURENSA: Is dit hoe jy uitgevind het wat gebeur het? // SUBTITLES: Is that how you found out? RICHARD: Dis hoe ek uitgevind het, ja. // SUBTITLES: That's how I found out, yes. VO: A haunting discovery on a remote Mozambican beach… UPSOUNDS: NEWS INSERTS NEWS 1: A burnt wreckage and nothing else. What happened… NEWS 2:… extensive search and investigations to try to locate the two missing men and to piece together what has happened. NEWS 3:…an ominous sighting that suggests foul play. VO: John and Visser were nowhere in sight. UPS: Uh, probably 30, 40 metres from the boat. VO: Marcus Joubert, owner of a fishing charter in Mozambique, was among the first to arrive at the scene. We met him in the coastal town of Ponta do Ouro. UPS: MARCUS JOUBERT INTERVIEW: The way that I found the boat, it just sent shivers down my spine, and I knew that that boat was burnt on the beach, it wasn't burnt at sea. VO: Marcus was convinced this wasn’t the work of an experienced skipper. UPS: MARCUS: The motors were still in gear. If John had burned that boat, the motors would have been in neutral...So these are all small little things that I concluded to say that a skipper didn't beach this boat. UPS: CHERIE INTERVIEW LOURENSA: Initially when you still had hope and you didn't quite know what had happened to John, what role did social media and the community play in trying to find John? CHERIE: Enormous. Absolutely an enormous, enormous role… I mean, the story about John Matambu travelled like wildfire. It became an international story, an intercontinental story, that it was on the Washington Post. VO: Visser’s image was widely shared online. UPS: MARCUS: Right, now we’ve got a picture, we’ve got a name and it’s on social media VO: Then, four days after the boat was discovered, a breakthrough: UPS: MARCUS: Once we apprehended Visser…. It was, it was unbelievable how that happened. It was like watching a movie. VO: Visser had been tracked down in Mozambique’s capital, Maputo. Not by the police, but… the community. Richard went to Maputo to identify Visser. UPS: LOURENSA: Hoe was hy in daai oomblik gewees? RICHARD: Hy kyk nie vir my nie. Nee, hy is... LOURENSA: Emosieloos? Richard; Heeltemal.Toe vra hulle vir my of ek vir hom 'n vraag wil vra. Toe sê ek ja, ek wil net by hom weet waar's John? Toe sê hy vir my, nee, hy het John R20 000 gegee en John het hom in Ponta afgelaai en daarna weet hy nie verder nie. VISSER THE CRIMINAL REFLECTIVE LINK: So, I’m just going through a list of all the charges that’s been brought against Ferdi Visser over the years, it’s quite extensive and it crosses borders. It includes theft, common assault, fraud, more common assault… VO: Many of these cases are still open. UPS: PAUL MOSTERT INTERVIEW: He obviously knows that he's got the might of the law ahead of him. VO: Paul Mostert, a former police detective, assisted in Visser’s arrest 3 years ago. UPS: PAUL MOSTERT: He was a very clever guy. He knew how to manipulate people. He knew how to win your confidence over. And he knows how to get himself out of a lot of stuff. I received numerous of calls from a lot of guys throughout South Africa that were taken with fraud by Ferdi Visser and I roughly added it up. It came very close to about 8 or 9 million rand. VO: Many questions remain about Visser’s motives. Could he be running from more than just the law? COURT LINK: Following his arrest in Mozambique, Visser was extradited and was scheduled to appear in court in KZN in late May last year. John’s family, friends and other supporters travelled from near and far, determined to see Visser in court. UPS CROWD: Legend of Sodwana! VO: Our producers were there too. UPS VOX POPS: Producer: So why are you two here today? Janine: To see Visser and to see if we can get some answers from him. Frank: I want to know what they do to John Matambu VO: John’s supporters waited… but Visser never arrived. VO: The hearing proceeded despite Visser’s absence. He was facing charges of fraud and the theft of the boat. UPS: MAGISTRATE: The accused in the matter is Thomas Frederick Visser, VO: John’s supporters were dealt another unexpected blow. UPS: MAGISTRATE: The charges against the accused are withdrawn in absentia. UPS: People in the crowd shouting: What? Are you serious? No way! All chant: Justice for John! VO: Visser had allegedly injured himself on the way to court. UPS: CHERIE: And today, the coward didn't face us. He hit his head so that they would take him to our hospital because he couldn't face us, so that's what we're dealing with. UPS: JANINE: Bring him back here, now, today. JANINE: Patch him up and bring him back. JANINE: We’re here! VO: The fraud and theft charges were withdrawn after the authorities bungled the extradition, moving Visser from Mozambique back into South Africa. VO: Though the NPA confirmed the investigation is still ongoing it was devastating news for John’s friends and family. UPS CHERIE: We know the only person who knows what has happened to John is this man Visser and we handed him to the authorities on a platter… UPS CHERIE INTERVIEW: We just needed the system to do its job. And the system let us down in every way. Lourensa: Is that why you decided to contact Advocate Gerrie Nel? Cherie: Yes, 100%. VO: Gerrie Nel, who famously prosecuted disgraced Paralympian, Oscar Pistorius, now represents John Matambu’s family. UPS: GERRIE INTERVIEW Gerrie: We then met with Cherie and she, she compiled an impressive docket. Lourensa: What went wrong with the extradition? Do we know? Gerrie: We don't know, and I wish we did. If something goes wrong, we start playing the blame game. The NPA would say, we blame the police. The police would say, we blame the NPA. Where as they should all work together to ensure that justice is done. VO: The NPA confirmed that proper extradition procedures weren’t followed. They were not made aware of Visser’s arrest in Mozambique. VO: Because Visser had absconded from his parole, he was sent back to prison to serve the remainder of his original fraud sentence. VO: For months, Cherie and Adv. Nel pushed for something more. Not just justice… but accountability. VO: They believed there was enough evidence to open a murder case. UPS: GERRIE INTERVIEW It's really easy. Two people got on a boat. One got off. Where's the other one? VO: And then — just as it seemed they might be getting somewhere with John’s case — UPS: CHERIE INTERVIEW I then received a phone call from the investigation officer to say I have bad news… I’m sorry…(CRYING) ESCAPE LINK: Visser had escaped. Again. By the time authorities acknowledged it, he already had a 6-week head start. UPS JANINE INTERVIEW LOURENSA: Have you lost faith in the authorities? JANINE: Oh, ja. Yeah. No faith in them, ja.. LOURENSA: How does that make you feel? JANINE: Disgusted, absolutely disgusted that he's actually out of jail. That he was paroled. It should never have happened. But that's the justice system. VO: In February this year, nearly a year after John disappeared, authorities finally acted. VO: The South African Police Service confirmed they’ve closed the missing persons case, opened a murder investigation, and obtained a warrant for Visser’s arrest. UPS: Singing in background: John, John, John, John Matambu, the legend of Sodwana Bay.. VO: A murder case may finally be open — but for John Matambu’s loved ones, it’s far from closure. The suspect remains at large, and the system continues to fail those left behind. UPS: CHERIE IN GARDEN: LOURENSA: So this is what you brought back from Mozambique? This is the wreck? Cherie: It's just so tragic that it's gone from being his office to being your word, a wreck. It's more than that. This is John's coffin. LOURENSA: And if you could say anything to Ferdi Visser? CHERIE: I would tell him that he's not going to get away with murder. I now understand where the expression comes from. It comes from the broken justice system. It comes from people like Ferdi Visser who are repeat criminals, who know that they can fly under the radar because the justice system isn't together enough to bring them in and apprehend them. And I would tell him that he picked the wrong fisherman, that he picked the legend of Sodwana and he made a big mistake. UPS: John Matambu: Let’s go boys! Thank you.

metadata.Summary: A respected fisherman. A fugitive on the run. A boat that vanished—only to resurface, torched and abandoned on a remote Mozambican beach. This is not just a story about a man who disappeared at sea. It’s a story about a system that failed—again and again. In this investigation, Carte Blanche exposes the glaring gaps in the justice system that allowed convicted fraudster Ferdi Visser to manipulate the law, evade parole, and escape custody—not once, but twice. How did a known fugitive manage to slip through the cracks so easily? And with Visser still on the run, will authorities finally be held accountable?
